It's true this game's launch was awful. But at the time of writing this, the game is absolutely incredible. If you even find the setting of the game mildly interesting, you should give it a try. The level of polish between now and when the game launched is night and day. 

The roleplay elements are super extensive and the variety you can have in the story and the gameplay is massive between the huge amount of dialogue, guns, cyberware, eta. Not to mention the DLC is also amazing with the new ending options and the characters and their choices are incredibly compelling. 

The game is still not perfect, I did run into some bugs during my most recent playthrough however non of them were game-breaking like they were at launch. Performance is also a hitch for low to medium end PCs, I would suggest getting used to DLSS and frame gen if you are on an RTX card although I can't speak for AMD users. I will also say that CDPRs take on a FPS is a little clunky at times and can be quite noticeable when doing stuff like sliding. And finally this is an RPG at heart so if you don't like large amounts of straight up just talking and picking dialogue choices you may find yourself bored or frustrated sometimes. 

However as a person who mostly plays FPS, the content of the story was sufficient to keep me from being bored, especially as someone who really likes the setting and genre of Cyberpunk. So if you like that too you should give it a try.

While Phantom Liberty was a great expansion, the update that was released alongside it absolutely ruined the game. 
They made all skill checks and areas scale with your character. The idea was to remove early level restrictions from the map and open up the entire city from the start. Which was just never a problem. The idea as a whole is just counterintuitive. It's basic game logic that the areas closer to big bads should be higher tier. And progressing towards them is half the fun of these types of open world games. Plus, it wasn't like leveling to keep up while exploring was remotely difficult or problematic in any way.
This change wasn't just unnecessary, it also ruins the experience as a whole. Your character now feels less competent the more you level, actively punishing you for exploration, and it restricts your character building by FORCING you into specialized builds.
Now this can be fixed with a mod and the game is still great otherwise, but I could never recommend a game that requires a mod to feel playable. 

TLDR: 2.0 ruined the game by punishing exploration and forcing character specialization, this is fixable through mods, but screw the developers for doing this to begin with.

I anticipated, played, and repeatedly completed  Cyberpunk 2077 at release (via GOG). I even took two weeks off work to fully take in the experience on PC, using my then brand-new RTX 2060 Super. It was certainly an experience, but a mixed one. The game had various bugs and glitches and wasn't stable at all. With a little humor, I was still able to have a great time and ignore most of the technical issues.

Almost 6 years later, I gave it another try and HOLY MOLY it's a completely different game. It has fully reached the potential people saw back then. Even more than that, the developers turned it into a masterpiece.

The game can run on a wide variety of systems thanks to its highly customizable graphics settings. I tried out every setting to make it run as smoothly as possible on my build. That experience alone was fun as heck. I truly understand why this game is one of the great benchmark titles for PC hardware. It looks absolutely stunning, especially considering its age. There isn't much more that needs to be said about the graphics and performance.

The skill system seems to have been massively overhauled. Combined with your cyberware, the game now lets you create genuinely distinct builds with depth. I chose to play as a gunslinging cowboy, focused on ridiculous headshot damage and a high cool attribute. There are also many dialogue options tied to your attributes. Having certain attributes at a high level unlocks a surprising number of unique dialoge options, encouraging multiple playthroughs. In some way, this has always reminded me of Fallout NV, which is a huge compliment. I also see great potential in a Netrunner build for my next playthrough.

The story and the overall pacing are peak. I love how naturally the relationships between V, Johnny and all the other main characters develop. Keanu is a real gem and the star of the game. The choices you make genuinely matter. The world feels believable and immersive enough to lose yourself in for hours. I also love how the police and wanted system was overhauled, too.

My only gripe with the game is the long introduction [spoiler] that builds your relationship with Jackie. By my x-th playthrough, I started noticing- and hating- how hard the developers try to make him as sympathetic as possible, just to make you care even more when he dies.

Bro... I'm tired of getting my heart broken.

RIP, Jackie.[/spoiler]

It is, without a doubt, a masterpiece. Have fun playing it!

h1]Cyberpunk for me was one of the most immersive and engaging open world videogame experiences i've ever had[/h1] ,

While this might sound like a pretty loaded statement I stand behind it.

There are other games that of course felt sort of similar to me.

But the whole package here makes something that is greater than it's parts.

I still remember my first time playing Cyberpunk2077.

Little things like entering a car and having the cutscene play out [b]in the car and in first person[/b] while driving through an open world listening to the car radio.

Everything at 1/1 scale.

And everything is [b]huge[/b].

I couldn't remember another game where the buildings are literally as tall and wide as mountains from metal and painted with neon. And they managed it to make them feel like you are sort of scouring through them by walking through underpasses and tunnels, over and under bridges, up and down elevators and ladders etc.

Or just walking through Urmland Street, walking through your small part of the Megabuilding, visiting Lizzies, the first time at Clouds all these things are so vividly realized and felt so tangible.

The character models are incredibly high fidelity, the materials of the clothes, the cyberware the way they animate [b]chefs kiss[/b]

Also I really appreciate the story of both the main game and the DLC.

The world building is superb and I think that the MO of CDPR licensing already established IPs and making a game from it while also having world class writers writing high quality stories and characters for it is beyond genius.

Depending on how you play, your gameplay experience can also be surprisingly varied.

Either covert hacking from a distance or hacking in combat.. or even both. Want to simultaneously use tech weapons with it? no problem.

Or do want it to be more action orientated with down to earth shotguns, revolvers and SMGs?

[i]How about no hacking?[/i]

Scared the cameras could ruin your ninja run?

Just install Sandy and Camouflage. Level up your engeneering perk a bit and run directly in front of cameras to turn them off and dash back to your hiding place while the world stands still.

Finishing off the remaining enemies with throwing knifes and katana before they even notice.

I love what they did here gameplay wise.

The addition of the forward dash and double jump was also a big brain move for traversal. This makes it feel a tiny bit like a parkour game in some aspects because the architecture encourages you to climb through it.

Exploring the open world and finding interesting notes, quests, weapons and upgrade materials in unconventional places really encourages you to look at every corner of this beautifully realised ♥♥♥♥ hole of a cyber city where the machine of capitalism went out of control.





After all that praise I have a nitpick though.

Given that this is a huge open world game with lots of moving parts there is bound to be some wear and tear.

One thing I notice every run is that when you see your own character in a cutscene like in the very beginning or very end of the game it always looks inferior to the characters you meet along the story.

Especially the face animations.

Makes some sense because you can style your character in many different ways but it always stands out to me like a sore thumb.

yeah.. other than that I have not many notes considering how much they already patched.

I mean there is always something one could criticize but at some point I feel there should be acceptance of things that are not bugs.

And I'm sure that when CDPR goes in the second round with Orion, there will be changes made that will fix, expand and improve upon alot of things that me and other people would appreciate for Cyberpunk.

The negative review is for this: Do not buy it at full price, especially not if you have a mid-range PC like mine AND especially if you are a completionist like me. I tried to experience all the content the game had to offer in a single playthrough, which led to me "optimizing" it (meaning completing all side jobs, fixer gigs and NCPD scanners). Here is my extensive review:

Six years after its original release, I thought the game would be in a pretty great state, but it is still pretty disappointing. I think most people who praise it, they do so because they compare it to the dumpster fire it was on release. But the game still feels unpolished, even unfinished, and it's still riddled with bugs. Not game-breaking ones, but they are still there. I had to install numerous mods in order to get to a decent playable state (fix for junky melee combat, pedestrian behaviour, quality of life elements for HUD and menus, like filters etc, de-scaled skill checks which were impossible after leveling up)

Gameplay wise, the RPG elements are minimal, the dialogue options are mostly different flavours of the same choice, the combat is repetitive and the enemy AI is extremely stupid, even in Very Hard difficulty. The side content (gigs and NCPD scanner jobs) are all duplicate brain-dead quests (read flavour text, go to location, sneak/shoot, loot chest, read flavour text). And no, the city is not immersive at all for me. All the places feel the same.

Its only redeeming quality, the story and characters, are overshadowed and diluted by the immense amount of mediocre side content that continuously distracts you (text messages, calls, etc) and forces you to engage with it ("wait for a whole day until the next mission objective", "find something else to do until [character] contacts you"). 

As always, I think the level design would have benefited if was a more linear and condensed experience, allowing the player to progress through the map gradually and learning to organically traverse through the levels, instead of blindly following quest markers.

I'm considering playing it again and focusing only on the main mission, just to experience the story in a more condensed way, but I am dreading the thought of having to go through all the tedious character progress and repetitive combat.

EDIT: I played the game again, and engaged only with the main quest. It was a far more enjoyable experience for 2 reasons: 1) I was already accustomed with the in-game universe (slang, concepts, characters) and I realized this was part of why I felt lost all the time during my first playthrough, and 2) I was not distracted by the side content and I was able to focus on the story and characters).

Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game but its held down by the open world elements that feel they were forced and rushed by the devs, because apparently these are the minimal expectations for a AAA release.

I love CD Projekt. The Witcher is one of my greatest loves, and The Witcher 3 in particular, despite its notoriously messy launch, remains one of the defining games of my life. Noblesse oblige, however, Cyberpunk 2077 took that predicament to an entirely different level. Its release seemed beyond redemption, yet the Poles worked what can only be described as magic. 

The result is a monumental work, one whose attention to detail borders on the pathological. It builds a world of extraordinary corporeality, an immersion unlike anything else the medium has to offer. Night City is a monster to be feared, one that inevitably takes everything from you while offering only fleeting shards of humanity in return. It is a city haunted by nostalgia for a present that is constantly slipping through its inhabitants' fingers, suspended between helplessness and hopelessness. What keeps people moving is the belief that, amid everything that is lost, memories, bonds, decisions, and actions can still endure. Beneath layers upon layers of steel, the only thing left worth preserving is identity. 

It is no coincidence that the story revolves around the Relic. The Soulkiller represents libertarianism's ultimate fantasy: stripping human beings of their souls so they can be fully subordinated to capital, while those in power preserve themselves by erasing the last remaining limit to domination, mortality itself. Everyone knows this is the system they are condemned to inhabit, yet awareness doesn't necessarily imply submission. Night City devours people, and those unable to cope with its tremendous injustices gradually abandon their humanity, finding meaning in their suffering through wealth, power, and recognition. Cyberpunk 2077 is intellectually rich in its philosophical ambitions, but even richer in the way it communicates them: not through mere exposition, but by making you live them. 

Sorrowfully, the gameplay has significant shortcomings. Several of its core systems may feel unfair, unbalanced, or simply underdeveloped. The driving is simply and utterly dreadful and, as someone who avoids fast travel whenever possible, it became one of the game's greatest obstacles, even if the wide variety of vehicles and their distinct handling characteristics soften the blow somewhat. Progression is unbalanced, trivializing everything far too soon. Looting is another unnecessary problem the game creates for itself, one that could have been solved in countless better ways, especially without forcing the player to rely so heavily on the scanner. Combat, meanwhile, never quite lives up to its potential. Even on the highest difficulty, it rarely feels demanding, and despite its impressive breadth of builds and playstyles, it lacks the mechanical depth and satisfaction I had hoped for. The sheer amount of freedom is admirable, but that freedom inevitably comes at a cost.

You might think it contradictory to praise Cyberpunk 2077 so highly while acknowledging such fundamental mechanical flaws, but great games are not always defined by the perfection of their systems. What impressed me most is not any individual component, but the extraordinary cohesion between them. Every artistic discipline serves the same emotional and thematic purpose: portraying a  vision of a world where identity itself could become a commodity. Its branching narrative, world-building, unforgettable cast, dialogue, animation, staggering level of immersion, and the unmistakable passion poured into every corner of the experience elevate it far beyond the sum of its mechanics. Its dystopian vision feels unparalleled, while its lore reveals itself through countless interconnected threads. It has the rare ability to leave you emotionally devastated before quietly offering comfort in the same breath. Its visual identity is outstanding. Phantom Liberty is exceptional. The soundtrack is phenomenal in both composition and implementation, and in the way it interacts with the rest of the work. Its thoroughgoing mise en scène extracts the maximum expressive potential from every scene. [spoiler]The Sun ending, with V gazing toward the Crystal Palace as the chorus of "Never Fade Away" begins to swell, made me think: "There goes something truly special."[/spoiler].

I absolutely love Cyberpunk 2077. It is one of the very few video games that left me with a profound sense of emptiness, the distinct feeling that I would never experience anything like it again. That is transcendence.

A thing of beauty, I know
Will never fade away

 I was one of those people who wrote this game off years ago after its disastrous launch. It took lots of convincing from multiple friends for me to finally give this game a shot (once the game + DLC went on deep sale). I am glad I waited all these years for the game to be ironed out and fixed, but I also feel like I have missed out on something the past few years. I have just completed the game + DLC after 75 hours, and left a lot of side missions and gigs on the table in the base game and have been told there are a lot of small things I missed, but that content can wait for a second playthrough eventually.

It took me awhile to get into the game, roughly 10-15 hours before it finally hooked me and made me want to come back and keep playing. The characters are fun and enjoyable to speak and interact with. I do wish there were more characters to develop friendships/relationships with but there are still plenty by modern game standards. I think Mass Effect has just ruined my expectations in terms of relationships/companions in video games. There is a heap of side characters that give you side jobs/gigs and some of them are genuinely really funny and interesting. The main story has plenty of twists and turns depending on how you do things in what feels like a way most games nowadays do not do, which gives this game probably hundreds of hours of replayability to those who really sink into this. I think there is something along the lines of 7 or 8 endings for this game so, there are plenty of ways to tackle the main narrative of the game.

The game's build variety is top notch. I feel like I barely scratched the surface of the possibilities. I opted to do a more run and gun shoot first and ask questions later style. The gun play is smooth and all of the different ranged/melee weapons feel unique and different with various upgrades and attachments. I ended up using the same few guns for most of my playthrough but mainly because I just enjoyed them so much. The hacking in the game is something I wish I invested in a bit more for my first playthrough, as there are some seriously game breaking whacky stuff you can do with it. Exploring the hacking more will have to wait for my second playthrough. 

The game has plenty of vehicles and character apartments to choose from and purchase. Admittedly I did not really spend time exploring this stuff because I was just enjoying playing the game but now that I finished the game and am rich, ill go back and take a look at all of that stuff. Driving in the game feels just ok? Its nothing to write home about. Feels very GTA-like. The cops in the game are a complete afterthought which is disappointing. A lot of the time the cops just spawn behind/in front of you once you get wanted which just feels bad/lame. Feels like a missed opportunity to have cool chrome-juiced cops tracking you down or doing anything other than trying to chase you. If you break line of sight, they forget about you very quick. The cops really only care once you start killing civilians or once you ram a cop car. Speeding and breaking road laws right in front of them does nothing. 

This review is already really long. If you like immersive RPGs, big open worlds, cyberpunk aesthetic and large branching narrative games you will enjoy this game. Getting the base game + DLC on sale for roughly $30 feels like a really good deal. This is not a game without faults, but its a good ride.

I never reviewed this??? It's a masterpiece. Flawed, but what masterpiece isn't? The worldbuilding is glorious. The architecture tells its own story. The narrative is chef's kiss. The voice acting is top notch. The music is perfection. It's the kind of game where, when the credits roll, I sit in a stunned stupor after the game ripped me apart to my bare atoms and left me to deal with it. There are many different endings so be prepared to be broken over and over. It's one of those games that's clawed around in my mind and left marks that will last forever. 

Think of every negative thing in modern media and crank it up by 1000% while the world is limping towards a total collapse, and give it more tech. That's Cyberpunk 2077's backdrop. 

I didn't expect the story to revolve around V with a dead rocker boy in her head. I was annoyed by it at first. Silverhand pissed me off. I played on PC at launch so I ran into very few bugs.  My car got stuck under the map when I called it, and I once looked away from my parked bike for a second and it launched into V like it was possesed and slammed into a vending machine. Those are old bugs I haven't seen again. 

The immersive city and stories are everything. The world is too close to reality and it knows it. The satire on current society is spot on from the ads, the TV commercials and shows, the trash, the districts themselves, healthcare, police, and more. The casual background TV shows are fascinating satire. Each channel pushes a different narrative in the interest of a different corporation. Like fox vs cnn. The host always controls the narrative. When it seems to be slipping from him, he reins it back in like a noose to align with the show's narrative and protect that channel's corporate aligned interest. If it puts someone's life in danger then damn them without a thought. Neither side has the publics interest in mind. It's all personal corporate interest that will destroy everything in its path until it eats its own tail.

The game is depressing. There are no happy endings. V's narrative isn't about saving a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world. Raging against the Cyberpunk society thus far has only gotten people killed and changed nothing. It's about what personally matters to you and how you choose to live. Even if that choice is to rage for one moment before being snuffed out. Helping someone else live a little longer, going quietly into the good night, or making a deal with a devil. I love it because it leaves a mark and sticks with me far longer with resounding thoughts than a neatly wrapped happy ending.

The way the game gets you so attached to each person you met and form a connection with is insane. Even the rockerboy that lives inside your head. I smiled, laughed and cried with each character and my intercations with them. It's like you're truly living V's life. To me, that's what makes a game worth remembering and replaying. Cyberpunk is up there with Baldur's Gate 3 for me cause of that. The gameplay itself is also very enjoyable! I spent most my time running around Night City and Dogtown doing side quests, gigs, NCPD Scanner hustles, etc and forgetting that I probably should do that main questline at some point. Of course, the game has flaws just like every game tends to have but I think the pros outweigh the cons for this game. Cyberpunk 2077 and it's DLC is worth giving a try if it interests you!

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that not only entertains but also immerses you completely. Night City feels alive in a way that most open worlds do not achieve. The city watches you, tempts you, overwhelms you, and sometimes quietly breaks you.

The 2.0 overhaul has transformed the game significantly. Combat is now sharp, fluid, and expressive. Whether you’re slicing through time with a Sandevistan, causing chaos through hacking, or going full chrome with cyberware, every character build feels meaningful. The gunplay carries weight, melee combat feels brutal, and the city reacts to your presence.

The story is the real draw. V’s journey is personal and existential, avoiding the typical “save the world” formula. The dynamic between Johnny Silverhand and V is messy, magnetic, and unforgettable. The side characters feel like real individuals with genuine stakes, rather than mere quest markers.

Phantom Liberty takes everything to its peak. Dogtown is dense and dangerous, the choices you make carry more weight, and Idris Elba’s performance as Solomon Reed is outstanding. The new endings add emotional depth that lingers long after the credits roll.

Visually, the game is stunning, especially on a powerful PC. Path tracing makes Night City resemble a neon cathedral. The soundtrack embodies pure cyberpunk with its industrial, electronic, and atmospheric qualities, perfectly complementing the experience.

Cyberpunk 2077 may not be flawless, but it is undeniably powerful. It is stylish, brutal, beautiful, and profoundly human beneath all the chrome.

For me, this game is not just a playthrough; it’s an experience that stays with you.

Set in a future where people have found ways to cheat death, lose themselves in ecstasy simulations and indulge in every imaginable convenience, the game instead puts you in the shoes of a dying protagonist, which makes it a very bold and thought provoking premise. Along the journey, you meet memorable characters who act remarkably real and the relationships you develop with them feel organic. And in the grand scheme of things, the search for meaning and spirituality continues.

In retrospect, these themes are nothing new to the cyberpunk genre, but CDPR managed to deliver a tight narrative and deeply immersive experience as a perfect love letter to the genre with countless details and references scattered throughout the world, making it a fun and one-of-a-kind game to lose yourself in. With how the story hits the nail on the head on many subjects regarding our current world: the gradual takeover of government institutions by corporations, the rise of AI and its growing impact on livelihoods, and the alarming loss of meaningful human connections,... the story can only resonates even more than when the game first launched. This is precisely why Cyberpunk 2077 remains such a beautiful experience, one that will never fade away from memory.

TLDR: Having been overhyped before launch and apparently released in a poorly optimised state, the game suffered initial poor critics. However, as it is now, it is a great, if only good to some, game. Does it compare to Witcher 3? No. Is it a completly different genre? Yes. So maybe quit comparing the 2 and enjoy it for what it is; a 2077 tale of how much can go wrong in a heist and how will you ever manage to fix it.

Story: As V, choose from 3 selectable backgrounds (which barely impacts the game), you decide you've had enough of your old life and decide to make it big in Night City. I'll try to skim the details and bite into the obvious fat; Johnny Silverhand, a.k.a. our dear Keanu Reeves. He does a good job, like amazingly so. He basically carries the whole story on his back. Honestly, if it wasn't for his annoying naggy personna in the game, I would've chosen many different dialogue choices, and from this comes the main gimmick of the game. Balance between the main protagonist, and Johnny. 

Gameplay: Guns feel tight and there is variety, though most scopes look horrendous.
While I was initially overwhelmed by the amount of details and possible interactions at any given time... I quickly realised that the actual worth of said interactions are minimal. So apart from looting chests and kills, hacking and interacting with NPCs related to quest, there's no reason to fiddle with everything. This is an obvious case of quantity over quality.
Stealth is amazingly well done for how little they push it to be used... There are many ways to go about it; using TVs, cameras, vending machines, etc to distract enemies, turning off CCTVs with enough tech knowledge manually, by hacking it, or simply by finding the right terminal. You can knock out enemies if you catch them unaware and hide their bodies in lockers and dumpsters, and much, much more.
While there is a level cap (both street cred and proper), I never saw an enemy's level. My guess is that this was changed in an update, and I'm unsure if it was the right call. It allows the player to go wherever and whenever, sure, but renders the whole experienced a bit disjointed.  
Some objectives grant better rewards if you don't outright kill enemies, and while there are means to knock out enemies without killing them, accidentaly killing them is too easy. More specific weapons that don't kill with an extra bullet would have been nice. 
There are well over 200 side quests (gigs, psychos and sidejobs). Depending on your backstory and previous choices, you may or may not have access to some, at least not on a singular playthrough. This is excluding the NCPD hustles... aaaand this is excluding the DLC. Yeah there's a lot to do. But not all is really worth doing.
The character customisation at the beginning is pretty in depth, but the game is mostly 1st person (well it 100% is, apart from driving). I would still say it's worth it since you can view yourself in some critical moments. It hits different when you haven't seen yourself in around 60 hours.
The cyberware section of the character is ''interesting'', as you can equip quickhacks (spells, if you like), and change some of your body up; enabling you to double jump, have blades coming out of your arms, equiping a thick boi skeleton and the likes. However it feels like a lot of the stats that the cyberware grants are superfluous. 
The perks and stats points, imo, is where its at, as it will impact how you approach missions, dialogue options, extra moves and even which weapons you're more proficient with.

Graphics: Cyberpunk is very demanding, probably due to how many things are going on at once. There is no loading between areas and since the city is built vertically with neons signs everywhere who can be flickering, playing different TV stations, NPCs interacting with each other through dialogue or pure fighting... There is a never ending demand of things towards your CPU. 
The game basically seems to have a hard time handling itself, much like Skyrim. Maybe their vision was too big for the tech of the time. 
But back to graphics.. The game looks great, especially important characters. NC truly becomes something when night comes. But then again, everything looks better in the dark ;)

Audio: The voice overs are amazing. Even V, the main protagonist, which you hardly ever see, manages to retain a strong presence with just dialogue. I don't think people realise how hard that is! 
The music is pretty good, however don't expect bangers. It's mostly industrial, tehcno and punk. While this might sound appealling, in kinda gets annoying and feels like just noise as it can get hard to isolate the music from the noise. There's no real chill moment, it's just noise, noise and noise. I remember a moment during a gig where the NPC in front of me was talking to me, someone phoned me and it automatically picked up, a small group of randoms were having a conversation next to me, my personnal radio (on the protagonist) was playing, a TV station was chatting on about some such and a portable radio was also playing. So... a quicksave was in order and I shot the place up. So yeah. sometimes too many dialogues are happening at once and can overlap each other. 
NC is lively, too lively for lil' ol' me. 

For a game that throws sex in your face all the time where there's romancing to be done, I had basically 4 options; to be gay, kinda gay, super gay, or straight with someone that keeps telling me to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I guess I'll deal with a nutcase but man... Really?! Was it that hard to have a 2nd option?!
My car also got stuck inside the road, doodads could drop from the sky (tires especially, dunno why), and Jackie's bike was launched in the stratosphere after getting stuck in a fence. Enemies can also sometimes drop stuff through the floor so you can't pick it up. Bummer. Also, I dunno if it's just me, but for once the traffic works right in a game!!! While I may have sounded like the game is litered with bugs, it's really minor and my game only crashed once. All the other things are minor.
There's also a ton of easter eggs, often very subtle. I also found Roach's minigame funny. Way too funny.
